import base64
from google.cloud import storage

# Generate and encode a 256-bit AES key (store this securely!)
import os
raw_key = os.urandom(32)  # 256 bits
encoded_key = base64.b64encode(raw_key).decode()

client = storage.Client()
bucket = client.bucket("my-secure-bucket")
blob = bucket.blob("sensitive-data.bin")

# Upload with customer-supplied encryption key
blob.upload_from_filename(
    "sensitive-data.bin",
    encryption_key=raw_key,
)

words.etymology: CSEK is a GCP acronym for Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys; the term parallels CMEK but emphasizes that the key material itself is supplied by the customer on each call rather than held in a managed key store.

words.shortDefinition: GCP's AI-driven recommendation engine that surfaces actionable cost, security, reliability, and performance recommendations across GCP services based on actual usage patterns.
words.simpleDefinition: Active Assist analyzes your GCP usage and emits specific, actionable recommendations: idle VMs to shut down, oversized disks to resize, IAM bindings to remove, and committed-use discounts to purchase. Recommendations appear in the Cloud Console and are also available via API for automated remediation.
words.longDefinition: Active Assist is the umbrella brand for GCP's recommender system — a collection of ML-driven analyzers that observe actual resource usage across a GCP project or organization and surface concrete improvement opportunities. Each recommender targets a specific service and concern area: the VM right-sizing recommender monitors Compute Engine instance CPU and memory utilization and suggests machine type downgrades; the IAM recommender identifies IAM role bindings that grant permissions never used in the past 90 days; the CUD recommender analyzes Compute Engine usage patterns and suggests optimal committed-use discount purchases; the unattended project recommender flags projects with no recent API activity; the firewall recommender identifies overly permissive firewall rules. Recommendations are surfaced in multiple places: the Cloud Console's Recommendations Hub, individual service pages, Insights API (machine-readable), and Security Command Center (for security-class recommendations). Implementing a recommendation typically requires one click in the Console or a single API call. The Active Assist ecosystem has expanded over successive Google Cloud Next events to cover cost, IAM, networking, reliability, and sustainability domains — evolving from reactive cost findings toward proactive risk scoring across the full operational surface.
words.connector: Think of Active Assist like a financial advisor who watches your spending every month and sends you a ranked list of specific changes — not 'spend less generally' but 'cancel the idle gym membership, downgrade the phone plan, switch to this credit card for travel' — with the action button right there.
words.techContext: Active Assist's IAM recommender identified 47 service account bindings with roles never exercised in six months; removing them reduced our IAM blast radius significantly.
words.exampleSentence: Active Assist caught a fleet of 23 idle development VMs that had been left running over a long weekend, surfacing a one-click shutdown recommendation that saved $4,000 in monthly spend.
words.etymology: Active Assist was introduced as a brand name at Google Cloud Next 2020, combining 'active' (ongoing, real-time analysis) and 'assist' (the service helps you take action rather than just reporting metrics).

words.shortDefinition: The Cloud Logging infrastructure that evaluates every log entry against filter-based routing rules and forwards matching entries to BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, or another GCP project.
words.simpleDefinition: The Log Router intercepts every log entry written to Cloud Logging and compares it against a set of sinks — each sink has a filter (which logs to match) and a destination (BigQuery dataset, Cloud Storage bucket, Pub/Sub topic, or another logging bucket). Matched entries are forwarded to the destination; unmatched entries stay only in the default _Default log bucket.
words.longDefinition: The Log Router is the routing layer within Cloud Logging that determines where log entries go after ingestion. By default, all log entries land in two built-in log buckets: _Default (most logs, 30-day retention) and _Required (admin activity and system event logs, 400-day mandatory retention). Log sinks allow routing a copy of any log subset to an external destination for purposes the built-in buckets cannot serve: long-term archival (Cloud Storage), analytical querying (BigQuery), real-time event processing (Pub/Sub), or cross-project aggregation (a central logging project). Each sink has three components: a filter (a Cloud Logging filter expression matching on log name, resource type, severity, labels, or any structured log field); a destination (the target service resource); and an identity (a service account automatically created by Cloud Logging with the minimum permissions needed to write to that destination). Log sinks are critical for compliance architectures that require log retention beyond Cloud Logging's 30-day maximum, audit trail export for SIEM integration (Splunk, Chronicle, QRadar consume from a Pub/Sub sink), and billing allocation log analysis via BigQuery. Aggregated sinks can be defined at the folder or organization level to centralize logs from all child projects.
words.connector: Think of Log Router and sinks like a postal sorting facility: every piece of mail (log entry) passes through the sorter, which reads the address fields (filter) and distributes copies to the right mail boxes (sinks) — BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub — while the original stays in the central post office.
words.techContext: We configured an aggregated sink at the organization level to forward all WARN and above logs to a central BigQuery dataset for our security operations team's SIEM queries.
words.exampleSentence: Our compliance audit required 7-year log retention; we created a Cloud Storage sink with a lifecycle policy to transition logs from Standard to Archive storage after 30 days.

codeExample.code:
# Create a BigQuery sink for audit logs from all projects in an organization
gcloud logging sinks create org-audit-sink \
  bigquery.googleapis.com/projects/central-logging/datasets/audit_logs \
  --organization=123456789 \
  --include-children \
  --log-filter='logName:"activity"' \
  --description="Organization-wide audit log sink to BigQuery"

# Grant the sink's service account write access to the BigQuery dataset
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding central-logging \
  --member="serviceAccount:$(gcloud logging sinks describe org-audit-sink \
      --organization=123456789 --format='value(writerIdentity)')" \
  --role=roles/bigquery.dataEditor

words.etymology: Log Router is a GCP-coined term for the internal routing component of Cloud Logging; 'sink' is a standard software architecture term for a destination that consumes data, borrowed from data pipeline and signal-processing vocabulary.

words.shortDefinition: A first-class Cloud Monitoring resource that encodes an SLI definition and SLO target, enabling continuous error budget calculation and burn-rate alerting.
words.simpleDefinition: An SLO object in Cloud Monitoring lets you declare your service level objective — 99.9% of requests succeed, p99 latency under 300 ms — and the platform computes your remaining error budget continuously. Burn-rate alerts fire when you are consuming budget faster than the window allows, before you breach the SLO.
words.longDefinition: Cloud Monitoring's SLO objects are native platform resources that implement the SLI/SLO/error budget model described in the Google SRE Book. You create an SLO object by specifying: the monitored resource (a Cloud Run service, GKE workload, or custom service); the SLI type (request-based availability — good requests divided by total requests — or window-based latency); the performance goal (for example, 99.5% of requests succeed); and the compliance period (rolling 30 days). Cloud Monitoring then continuously calculates the error budget (the allowed proportion of bad events within the window) and the current consumption rate. Burn-rate alerting is the key operational feature: rather than alerting when the SLO is breached (too late), burn-rate alerts trigger when the rate of budget consumption is high enough that the full budget will be exhausted before the window closes — days before a breach. A 14.4x burn rate for 1 hour, for instance, triggers an alert because it projects a full budget exhaustion within 72 hours. SLO objects integrate with the Error Budget Reports feature, providing a compliance view for regular reliability reviews. They also power the Service Dashboard in Cloud Console, making SLO health visible across an organization's service catalog.
words.connector: Think of an SLO object like a fuel gauge combined with a miles-per-gallon alert: instead of only telling you when the tank is empty (SLO breached), it warns you hours earlier that you are burning fuel 5x faster than the trip plan assumed.
words.techContext: We defined SLO objects for all fifteen production services and configured burn-rate alerts at 2x and 10x thresholds, giving our on-call team early warning before any user-facing SLO breach.
words.exampleSentence: The SLO object's 1-hour burn-rate alert fired at 2 AM, giving us three hours to fix a cache misconfiguration before our monthly availability SLO would have been breached.

codeExample.code:
# Create an availability SLO for a Cloud Run service
gcloud alpha monitoring slos create \
  --service=my-cloud-run-service \
  --project=my-project \
  --display-name="Checkout API 99.5% availability" \
  --request-based \
  --good-total-ratio-threshold=0.995 \
  --method=GET \
  --calendar-period=MONTH

# Set a burn-rate alert on the SLO
gcloud alpha monitoring slos set-burn-rate-alert \
  --slo=<slo-id> \
  --project=my-project \
  --burn-rate=14.4 \
  --lookback-duration=3600s

words.etymology: SLO stands for Service Level Objective, a term popularized by Google's SRE (Site Reliability Engineering) practice; the 'object' suffix indicates that GCP treats an SLO as a first-class, manageable resource in the Cloud Monitoring API.

words.shortDefinition: GKE worker nodes that run as Confidential VMs, encrypting all pod memory at the hardware level so that even the hypervisor cannot read it.
words.simpleDefinition: Confidential GKE Nodes apply Confidential VM technology to Kubernetes worker nodes: every node in the designated pool is an AMD SEV-protected VM. Pod memory is encrypted by the CPU with keys generated in hardware that Google's hypervisor and operations staff cannot access, providing TEE-level isolation for containerized workloads.
words.longDefinition: Confidential GKE Nodes extend Confidential Computing from the VM level to the Kubernetes workload level. In a standard GKE cluster, worker nodes are regular GCE VMs: their memory is visible to the hypervisor layer (and therefore in theory to a very privileged attacker or insider). Confidential GKE Nodes run each worker node as a Confidential VM — specifically an AMD SEV (Secure Encrypted Virtualization) instance — where the node's entire memory is encrypted by the AMD processor using a key that lives only in the processor hardware and is never exposed to Google's hypervisor, firmware, or operations staff. From Kubernetes' perspective, the nodes behave identically to standard GKE nodes: scheduling, networking, storage, and API access all function normally. The confidentiality guarantee applies at the node's memory boundary: data in pod memory, decoded TLS payloads, in-memory secrets, and ML model weights in VRAM are all encrypted at rest in DRAM. Confidential GKE Nodes are a GKE Enterprise feature. They are appropriate for regulated-industry workloads (financial AI inference, healthcare ML, cryptographic operations) where data-in-use protection is a compliance requirement. They can be combined with Binary Authorization and Workload Identity for a defense-in-depth Kubernetes security posture.
words.connector: Think of Confidential GKE Nodes like a filing cabinet in a locked safe inside a locked building: the building owner (Google) can access the building and the room, but the safe is sealed with a combination only the hardware knows, and the filing cabinet inside is yours.
words.techContext: We required Confidential GKE Nodes for our medical imaging inference workload because HIPAA required that PHI processed in memory never be accessible to cloud provider infrastructure.
words.exampleSentence: Enabling Confidential GKE Nodes for our ML serving pool let our compliance team certify that model inference over patient data satisfied our data-in-use protection requirements.

codeExample.code:
# Create a GKE cluster with a Confidential VM node pool
gcloud container clusters create my-confidential-cluster \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --machine-type=n2d-standard-4 \
  --enable-confidential-nodes \
  --project=my-project

# Add a Confidential GKE node pool to an existing cluster
gcloud container node-pools create confidential-pool \
  --cluster=my-cluster \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --machine-type=n2d-standard-8 \
  --enable-confidential-nodes

words.etymology: Confidential GKE Nodes directly mirrors the Confidential VMs product name; 'confidential' in this context is a hardware security term meaning the computation is protected from the platform operator via Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs).

words.shortDefinition: A zone-scoped, cost-optimized variant of Cloud Pub/Sub where you pre-provision throughput and storage capacity in exchange for approximately 10x lower per-GB pricing.
words.simpleDefinition: Pub/Sub Lite trades Pub/Sub's global replication and elastic scaling for a much lower price. You commit to a throughput and storage tier upfront, messages stay in one zone, and you pay roughly one-tenth the per-GB cost of standard Pub/Sub. Suitable for high-volume, predictable workloads where cost matters more than global durability.
words.longDefinition: Cloud Pub/Sub Lite is a separate messaging product from standard Cloud Pub/Sub, designed for high-throughput, cost-sensitive use cases where Pub/Sub's automatic elasticity and global replication are unnecessary. The architectural differences are significant: Pub/Sub Lite uses a partitioned, zone-scoped log model (similar to Apache Kafka's topic-partition model) rather than Pub/Sub's push-based, fully replicated global model. Capacity is pre-provisioned: you specify MiB/s of publish throughput, MiB/s of subscribe throughput, and GiB of storage at topic creation. Because there is no on-demand scaling and no global replication, Pub/Sub Lite achieves approximately 10x lower unit pricing than standard Pub/Sub for equivalent data volumes. Pub/Sub Lite supports backlog-aware subscriber scaling, message ordering within a partition, and seek-to-timestamp for replaying historical messages — capabilities absent from standard Pub/Sub. The primary use cases are log ingestion pipelines, event streaming for analytics, and IoT telemetry aggregation where message volume is predictable and sub-second global delivery guarantees are not required. Pub/Sub Lite is not suitable for workloads that need event fanout to many subscribers, require zone-failure tolerance, or have bursty, unpredictable throughput.
words.connector: Think of Pub/Sub Lite like a reserved lane on a highway versus on-demand rideshare: you commit to a specific lane capacity and pay a flat rate for it, which is far cheaper per-mile than summoning a car on demand — but you have no flexibility if your committed lanes are not enough.
words.techContext: We migrated our 500 GB/day IoT telemetry ingestion pipeline from standard Pub/Sub to Pub/Sub Lite, reducing messaging costs by 88% at the same throughput.
words.exampleSentence: Pub/Sub Lite was the right choice for our pipeline: throughput was predictable, messages stayed in us-central1-a, and the 10x cost reduction paid for itself in the first month.

codeExample.code:
from google.cloud.pubsublite.cloudpubsub import PublisherClient
from google.cloud.pubsublite.types import (
    CloudRegion, CloudZone, MessageMetadata, TopicPath
)

topic_path = TopicPath(
    project_number=123456789,
    location=CloudZone(CloudRegion("us-central1"), "a"),
    name="my-lite-topic",
)

with PublisherClient() as publisher:
    data = b"sensor-reading: 42.7"
    future = publisher.publish(topic_path, data)
    metadata: MessageMetadata = future.result()
    print(f"Published to partition {metadata.partition.value}, "
          f"offset {metadata.cursor.offset}")

words.etymology: Pub/Sub Lite appends 'Lite' — a common product naming convention indicating a reduced-feature, lower-cost variant — to the established Cloud Pub/Sub brand; launched in public preview in 2020.

words.shortDefinition: A GCP managed service for large-scale data movement into and between Cloud Storage buckets, from S3, Azure Blob Storage, HTTP sources, or on-premises filesystems.
words.simpleDefinition: Storage Transfer Service handles bulk data migrations to Cloud Storage without you managing transfer infrastructure. You configure a source (S3 bucket, Azure Blob container, another GCS bucket, or an on-premises agent pool), a destination GCS bucket, a schedule, and any filters — Google runs the transfer, handles retries, and reports results in the Cloud Console.
words.longDefinition: Storage Transfer Service (STS) is Google Cloud's managed data ingestion service designed for large-scale, reliable data movement into Cloud Storage. It covers three source categories: cloud-to-cloud transfers (from Amazon S3, Microsoft Azure Blob Storage, or other GCS buckets — all transferred across Google's backbone or the internet without requiring you to spin up VMs); URL-based transfers (from any HTTP or HTTPS endpoint that supports HEAD and GET — useful for public datasets or legacy HTTP fileservers); and on-premises or local transfers (using the STS agent, a Docker-based agent installed on local infrastructure that reads from local POSIX filesystems or NFS and streams to GCS). Transfers are configured as transfer jobs, which can be one-time or scheduled on a recurring basis (e.g., nightly sync of an S3 bucket to GCS). STS supports filtering by object name prefix or modification time, enabling incremental sync patterns. Transfer progress, byte counts, and error details are visible in the Cloud Console and can be exported to Cloud Monitoring. For on-premises transfers with high bandwidth requirements, the agent pool model supports multiple agents running in parallel across a local network. STS is the standard tool for cloud migrations, cross-cloud data replication, and routine data ingestion pipelines where managed infrastructure is preferable to DIY gsutil or aws s3 sync scripting.
words.connector: Think of Storage Transfer Service like a professional moving company for data: you tell them what to move, from where, to where, and on what schedule — they handle the logistics, loading, transport, and confirmation that everything arrived intact.
words.techContext: We used Storage Transfer Service to migrate 4 PB of archive data from Amazon S3 to Cloud Storage over six weeks, with nightly incremental syncs to catch any new objects added during the migration window.
words.exampleSentence: Storage Transfer Service completed our 200 TB S3-to-GCS migration with automatic retry handling; a DIY gsutil script had been failing intermittently for two weeks before we switched.

codeExample.code:
from google.cloud import storage_transfer

client = storage_transfer.StorageTransferServiceClient()

# Create a transfer job from S3 to GCS
request = storage_transfer.CreateTransferJobRequest(
    transfer_job=storage_transfer.TransferJob(
        project_id="my-project",
        description="S3 to GCS nightly sync",
        transfer_spec=storage_transfer.TransferSpec(
            aws_s3_data_source=storage_transfer.AwsS3Data(
                bucket_name="my-source-s3-bucket",
                aws_access_key=storage_transfer.AwsAccessKey(
                    access_key_id="AKIA...",
                    secret_access_key="...",
                ),
            ),
            gcs_data_sink=storage_transfer.GcsData(
                bucket_name="my-destination-gcs-bucket"
            ),
        ),
        status=storage_transfer.TransferJob.Status.ENABLED,
    )
)
job = client.create_transfer_job(request)
print(job.name)

words.etymology: Storage Transfer Service is a descriptive product name from Google Cloud; launched in 2015 as Google Cloud Storage Transfer Service to handle enterprise data ingestion and migration workloads at scale.

words.shortDefinition: An open-source FUSE adapter that mounts Cloud Storage buckets as local filesystems on Linux and macOS, enabling POSIX-style file access to object storage.
words.simpleDefinition: Cloud Storage FUSE (gcsfuse) mounts a GCS bucket as a directory on your machine. Applications that expect a regular filesystem path — reading config files, writing logs, loading ML model weights — can work against Cloud Storage without any code changes. Semantics are not full POSIX, but reads are fast for most workloads.
words.longDefinition: Cloud Storage FUSE (gcsfuse) is an open-source FUSE (Filesystem in Userspace) implementation maintained by Google that presents a Cloud Storage bucket as a mounted filesystem. When mounted, any process on the host can read and write to the bucket using standard filesystem calls (open, read, write, ls, cp) through the Linux or macOS kernel's FUSE interface. Under the hood, gcsfuse translates POSIX filesystem operations to Cloud Storage API calls: directory listings become object prefix list requests, file reads become partial object GET requests with range headers, and file writes become object PUT or compose operations. The semantics are not fully POSIX-compliant: there is no hard-link support, directory renames are non-atomic (they list and re-upload objects one by one), and write performance is lower than local disk due to the object-storage upload model. gcsfuse is most valuable for read-heavy workloads where data size exceeds local disk capacity: ML training jobs that load model checkpoints from GCS, Jupyter notebooks accessing large datasets stored in GCS, and batch processing jobs that read input files without modifying them. GKE and Cloud Run support gcsfuse via the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver, enabling pods to mount GCS buckets as volumes without running gcsfuse as a sidecar.
words.connector: Think of Cloud Storage FUSE like a translator at a border crossing: one side speaks filesystem language (your application), the other speaks object storage language (GCS), and gcsfuse translates in real time so both sides can communicate as if they were native speakers.
words.techContext: We mounted our model artifact bucket via the gcsfuse CSI driver in our GKE inference pods, loading 30 GB model weights directly from GCS without copying them to node local storage first.
words.exampleSentence: Cloud Storage FUSE let us run our legacy data processing application against a GCS bucket without modifying a single line of its filesystem access code.

codeExample.code:
# Install gcsfuse on a GCE VM (Debian/Ubuntu)
export GCSFUSE_REPO=gcsfuse-$(lsb_release -cs)
echo "deb https://packages.cloud.google.com/apt $GCSFUSE_REPO main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/gcsfuse.list
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install gcsfuse

# Mount a bucket
mkdir -p /mnt/my-bucket
gcsfuse --implicit-dirs my-bucket-name /mnt/my-bucket

# Use it like a regular filesystem
ls /mnt/my-bucket/
cp /mnt/my-bucket/model/weights.bin /tmp/weights.bin

words.etymology: FUSE stands for Filesystem in Userspace, a Linux kernel interface allowing filesystem implementations in user-space processes; gcsfuse is Google Cloud's specific FUSE implementation for Cloud Storage, open-sourced on GitHub.

words.shortDefinition: Google's standalone identity provider and directory service for organizations using GCP without Google Workspace, providing managed Google accounts, SSO, MFA, and device management.
words.simpleDefinition: Cloud Identity is the identity layer for GCP without the productivity apps. If your organization uses Office 365 or Slack but needs GCP access, Cloud Identity provisions managed Google accounts for your users and groups, integrates with your existing SAML or OIDC identity provider for SSO, and enforces MFA and device policy — so IAM has real, managed principals to bind to roles.
words.longDefinition: Cloud Identity is Google's enterprise identity-as-a-service offering, providing a managed Google account directory to organizations that use Google Cloud but have not adopted Google Workspace (formerly G Suite). The core value is a managed principal store: Cloud Identity lets organizations provision @yourdomain.com Google accounts for employees that are corporate-owned and centrally managed, rather than consumer @gmail.com accounts. These managed accounts are the principals that GCP IAM binds roles to, that BeyondCorp access policies evaluate, and that Cloud Audit Logs attribute actions to. Cloud Identity supports SAML 2.0 and OIDC federation — so organizations can configure SSO with Okta, Azure AD, Ping, or any SAML-compliant IdP, meaning users authenticate with their corporate credentials rather than a separate Google password. It also provides MDM (Mobile Device Management) capabilities for managing corporate iOS and Android devices, and conditional access policies (device trust, network location) that integrate with Identity-Aware Proxy and BeyondCorp Enterprise. Cloud Identity has a Free tier (basic accounts and SSO) and a Premium tier (advanced MDM, endpoint verification, and extended audit features). It is the identity foundation that makes GCP's IAM model enterprise-ready for organizations whose identity system of record is not Google.
words.connector: Think of Cloud Identity like a corporate badge issuance system: your building uses Google's access control infrastructure (GCP IAM), but Cloud Identity is the HR department that issues and manages the employee badges — your name on the badge comes from your own HR system (existing IdP) via SSO.
words.techContext: We set up Cloud Identity to give our GCP users managed Google accounts federated to our Okta IdP, so all GCP access was governed by our existing corporate SSO and MFA policies.
words.exampleSentence: Cloud Identity allowed us to provision GCP access for 300 engineers using their existing Okta credentials, without creating any consumer Google accounts or sharing service account keys.

codeExample.code:
# Verify Cloud Identity domain and list users via gcloud
gcloud organizations list

# List users in the Cloud Identity domain (requires Admin SDK access)
gcloud beta identity groups list --customer=my_customer_id

# List group memberships for a specific group
gcloud beta identity groups memberships list \
  --group-email=engineering@example.com

words.etymology: Cloud Identity is a compound of 'Cloud' (the GCP context) and 'Identity' (the IAM concept of who a principal is); Google separated the identity and directory features of Google Workspace into Cloud Identity as a standalone product in 2018 to serve organizations that needed GCP access without the productivity suite.
